\CRchapter{78}{The Count in Wood}{Days 285–287 · Frost 16–18, Y.H. 813}{Low Kiln, Sill}
\CRepigraph{The stick keeps what the slate cannot ask for, and the well keeps what the bucket does not take up; a count that stays in wood has paid nobody, and a thing left where it lies is still kept.}{A saying of the women at the yard well in Low Kiln, told of the firing-work and the weather}

\begin{CRchronicle}{78}
The sixteenth day of Frost came on in its own light. Under the Vail kiln-house roof in Low Kiln the boy lay carried and awake, two hundred and eighty-five days old by a count nobody kept, with one barley crust two inches from his ear and the empty place beside it unnamed. He took the body in the order the facts arrived — crust, gap, thread frozen in the dry heat and unwiped, cold stopped at cheek, temple and the bare wrist-joint, the afterdrop waiting past a warming nobody would perform. He knew a cold patient cannot clot and must be warmed slowly from the outside; the knowing bought him nothing at two inches of air. He wanted the crust lifted and could not close two inches on the pot handle. Both were true, and the second was louder.

Sella went to the fire before the basket and said \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would have said \emph{I}. She turned the coals with a broken pot, kept the charcoal unread, set the pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand, turned the dressed grain and gave it no figure, and left the widow’s mark untouched, for none of these is an opening. The yard went around its seven walked-around places with a look and a wide step and no number — the two unswept lines, the broken birth-slates, the pan’s gone ring, the skinned trough, the field’s empty place and the returning-line hand. The stayed frost lay white on the well lip and the plate of ice stood clouded with silt, and the yard called both weather.

On the seventeenth Ilva drew water at the well with the pail against her knee, clay pale in her nail crescents and rack dust in one thumb seam. To the woman who asked what the month’s firings had taken, now the district’s arithmetic had changed where two hundred stood, her hand went toward her sleeve and stayed there, and she answered: \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account.} The boy read her order of reaching and filed no tenth hand; the birch stayed in her sleeve.

On the eighteenth the file was turned out on the towel in the small hours as instruments on a tray — six hearings with no seventh, five askings with no witness, nine stoppings, nine hands, each on its own place with a finger between. The hand took the held interval and the empty interval, set them side by side and came down on the river’s low note. One hundred and fifty answers stood beside one hundred and forty-nine, exact and worth nothing at two inches of air; a round number did not stand up as a doctrine, for a doctrine is an account that has found a payer and none stood. The hand laid back against the fold, 287 stood exact and spoken by nobody, and the river went quiet. Nothing was opened, named, called, paid or ended.
\end{CRchronicle}
